title: A cheap, decades-old antidepressant just became one of the first real treatments for Long COVID fatigue
summary: A major randomized trial found a common, inexpensive antidepressant significantly reduces Long COVID fatigue — one of the first real treatments for a conditi...
content:
***Long COVID affects an estimated 65 million people worldwide, and for most of them, the defining symptom isn't respiratory — it's fatigue so persistent and disabling that it reshapes daily life. Until now, medical guidance for that fatigue has mostly amounted to pacing and symptom management, because no medication had strong trial evidence behind it. A new randomized trial just changed that, and the drug behind it is one you've probably heard of for a completely different reason.*** ## The trial The REVIVE-TOGETHER trial enrolled 399 adults in Brazil, all with significant fatigue lasting at least 90 days after a confirmed COVID-19 infection. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups for 60 days: fluvoxamine, an inexpensive antidepressant already widely used and sold as Luvox; metformin, a common diabetes drug; or a placebo. Both drugs had a real scientific rationale for being tested — but neither had actually been tried for this specific use in a rigorous trial before. ## What the results actually showed Fluvoxamine worked. Metformin didn't.

Two drugs went in with a plausible rationale. Only one came out with real evidence behind it.

By day 60, people taking fluvoxamine showed a significant reduction in fatigue compared to placebo, and that improvement held up through day 90. Patients on fluvoxamine were also nearly 50% more likely than the placebo group to report their fatigue had dropped to a mild level within just 30 days. Quality-of-life scores improved too, and side effects were actually less frequent with fluvoxamine than with either metformin or placebo. Metformin, despite earlier evidence that it can reduce the \*risk\* of developing Long COVID if taken during the initial infection, showed no benefit once fatigue was already established — the metformin arm of the trial was stopped early for futility. ## Why this result matters beyond the numbers This is being described as one of the first pieces of genuinely strong trial evidence for \*any\* Long COVID treatment — not a repurposed hope, not a small pilot study, but a proper randomized, placebo-controlled trial with a clear result. Fluvoxamine is also cheap and already well understood by prescribers, which matters enormously for how quickly a finding like this could actually reach patients compared to a brand-new, expensive drug still working through approval. ## The honest limits The trial only followed patients for 90 days, so it doesn't yet answer whether the benefit holds up over months or years. It also measured fatigue specifically — Long COVID often comes with a cluster of other symptoms, like brain fog and post-exertional malaise, that this trial wasn't designed to evaluate. Researchers are clear that Long COVID is a complex, multi-system condition, and one drug improving one symptom isn't the same as a cure. Still, for a condition that has offered patients very little beyond "manage it as best you can," a low-cost pill with a 99% statistical probability of outperforming placebo on fatigue is a genuinely meaningful data point — not a final answer, but the clearest evidence yet that this particular symptom is treatable. Sources:- Annals of Internal Medicine (REVIVE-TOGETHER trial); McMaster University; ScienceDaily; CIDRAP; Pharmacy Times.

title: Multi-cancer blood tests promised to catch cancer early. The first real trial data is in — and it's complicated.
summary: The first randomized trial of a multi-cancer blood test missed its main goal — but the data isn't a simple pass or fail, and here's why.
content:
***For years, the pitch behind multi-cancer early detection (MCED) tests has sounded almost too good: one blood draw, screening for dozens of cancer types at once, catching disease before symptoms even start. The best-known version, GRAIL's Galleri test, has been used by tens of thousands of people already. This year, the first results from the trial actually designed to test whether it works arrived — and the honest answer is: partly, in a more complicated way than the pitch suggested***. ## How it's supposed to work Galleri and tests like it look for tiny fragments of DNA that tumors shed into the bloodstream, along with patterns of chemical modifications on that DNA that differ between cancerous and healthy cells. If the test finds a signal, it also tries to predict where in the body the cancer is likely coming from, so doctors know where to look next. It's designed for the roughly 70% of cancer deaths that come from cancer types with no standard screening test at all — there's no routine blood test for pancreatic or ovarian cancer the way there is a mammogram for breast cancer. ## What the trial actually found The NHS-Galleri trial is the first large, randomized, controlled trial of an MCED test — 140,000 participants, the gold standard of medical evidence. Its main goal was to see whether annual Galleri screening would reduce the number of cancers caught late, at stage III or IV, when treatment options narrow and outcomes worsen. It didn't hit that goal. Overall late-stage cancer rates weren't significantly lower in the screened group.

A trial can miss its main goal and still teach something real — this is one of those cases.

But the results weren't nothing, either. Screening did shift some diagnoses earlier within that late-stage window — fewer cancers were caught at stage IV specifically, the most advanced and hardest to treat point. Screened participants also had fewer cancers discovered through emergency room visits or once symptoms had already appeared, which tend to be more advanced and harder to treat than anything caught by a scheduled screening. Separately, an even larger study — GRAIL's PATHFINDER 2, with nearly 36,000 participants — found that adding Galleri to standard screening (mammograms, colonoscopies, and so on) increased the total number of cancers detected 6.5-fold. ## Why the results read as mixed, not as a failure or a win Both things are true at once: the test didn't do the one specific job the trial was designed to prove (cutting late-stage diagnoses overall), and it did show real signals of benefit in more specific ways (shifting stage IV diagnoses earlier, cutting emergency-setting diagnoses, and finding more cancers overall when added to existing screening). Researchers involved in the trial have been careful to frame it as a genuine, informative result rather than a simple pass or fail — there's real data to learn from either way, not just a headline verdict. What's still missing is the outcome that matters most in the end: whether any of this actually helps people live longer. That requires longer follow-up than a 3-year trial can show, and it's the next thing researchers are watching for. ## Where things stand right now GRAIL completed its FDA approval application for Galleri in January 2026, and the test already carries the FDA's "Breakthrough Device" designation, which speeds up review for technologies addressing serious unmet needs. That doesn't mean approval is guaranteed or imminent — it means the review process is actively underway. In the UK, the NHS has said it will wait for the trial's fuller results before deciding whether to roll out MCED screening nationally. For now, Galleri remains available in the US only as an elective, out-of-pocket test — not yet an FDA-approved or insurance-covered screening tool, and not a replacement for existing recommended screenings like mammograms or colonoscopies. The honest takeaway from this year's data: multi-cancer blood tests are a real, promising direction — just not yet the settled, proven tool the early marketing sometimes implied. Sources: ASCO 2026 Annual Meeting presentations (NHS-Galleri trial, PATHFINDER 2 study); GRAIL press releases; Cancer Therapy Advisor; Clinical Lab Products.

title: A wristband that reads hormones without a blood draw — how close is Clair Health to actually working?
summary: A Stanford-founded startup raised $11.6M for a wearable that claims to track estrogen, progesterone, and cycle phase using sensors alone. Here's what the dev...
content:
*Most wearables that touch women's health are add-ons — a period tracker bolted onto a device originally built to count steps and measure sleep. Clair Health, a startup founded by two recent Stanford graduates, is pitching something different: a wrist-worn device built from the ground up around the hormonal cycle, rather than around a generic fitness-tracking chassis. The company just closed an $11.6 million seed round led by Khosla Ventures, with backers including 23andMe co-founder Anne Wojcicki, and plans to ship its first units in November*.

### What the device actually does

Clair's wristband packs in 10 biosensors — more than double what a typical smartwatch carries — including a biomagnetic sensor the company says isn't used in any competing consumer wearable. Instead of measuring hormones directly, the device reads physiological proxies: skin temperature, heart rate variability, and electrodermal activity. An AI model then runs those signals through more than 130 proprietary biomarkers to estimate levels of estrogen, progesterone, LH, and FSH, and to classify which phase of the menstrual cycle a person is likely in. A companion feature also analyzes short voice recordings during onboarding, aiming to pick up additional cycle-related signals from speech patterns.


This is an inference model, not a direct measurement — conceptually closer to how a continuous glucose monitor estimates blood sugar from interstitial fluid rather than drawing blood, than to an actual hormone panel. That's not automatically a flaw; CGMs proved indirect measurement can still be clinically useful. But it does mean the accuracy of Clair's output depends entirely on how well its models generalize across different bodies, cycles, and health conditions — something that's much harder to validate than a chemical assay.

### What the evidence says so far

The company reports 94% accuracy in classifying menstrual cycle phase, benchmarked against daily urine ovulation tests — a reasonable at-home comparison point, but not the same standard as a clinical blood hormone panel. In beta testing, Clair also says it identified nine distinct hormonal sub-phases, roughly double the four-phase model most health education still teaches. That's an intriguing claim, but "identified" here means detected by the company's own models, not confirmed against an external clinical gold standard.


Clair says it's launching an independent trial through Stanford's Gladstone BeeHive program, with a stated intent to publish peer-reviewed results. That trial — not the funding round — is really the thing worth watching. Until independent, published validation exists, the 94% figure and the nine-phase claim should be read as promising internal benchmarks rather than established clinical fact.

### Why it matters

Roughly a third of women have irregular cycles, which the company argues makes calendar-based period-tracking apps unreliable for a large share of users. Hormonal health has also long been underserved by wearable tech: most fitness devices were designed around metrics like heart rate and step count, with women's health features layered on afterward. If continuous, passive hormone monitoring works as described, it could give both patients and clinicians a much richer picture of cycle irregularities, perimenopause transitions, and conditions like PCOS or endometriosis than a single office visit and a patient's memory of symptoms ever could.


The company is explicitly launching Clair as a wellness product rather than a diagnostic one, with FDA clearance planned as a later step — a common path for consumer health wearables, but one that means the device isn't held to the same evidence bar as a regulated diagnostic tool at launch. For now, Clair is a genuinely novel approach to a real gap in women's health tracking — but the gap between "promising sensor data" and "something a doctor can act on" is exactly where independent validation, not funding announcements, does the real work.

title: "AstraZeneca’s Heart Disease Drug Fails Phase 3 Trial: What Went Wrong With Wainua?"
summary: AstraZeneca and Ionis’ Wainua (eplontersen) failed its Phase 3 ATTR-CM heart disease trial. Learn how the drug works, why the trial failed, and what it means...
content:
Category: Medical Research | Cardiology | Drug Development

# Introduction



A promising heart disease treatment developed by AstraZeneca and Ionis Pharmaceuticals has suffered a major setback after failing to achieve its main goal in a late-stage clinical trial.



The drug, ***Wainua (eplontersen)***, was being investigated as a potential treatment for **transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM)** — a rare but serious condition in which abnormal protein deposits accumulate in the heart and gradually impair its function.



The Phase 3  CARDIO-TTRansform trial failed to show a statistically significant reduction in cardiovascular deaths and recurring cardiovascular events compared with placebo, despite the drug showing a favourable safety profile.







### What Is ATTR-CM?



Transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy is a form of  **cardiac amyloidosis** , a disease caused by the buildup of misfolded transthyretin (TTR) proteins in heart tissue.



Normally, transthyretin is a transport protein produced mainly by the liver. However, in ATTR-CM, unstable TTR proteins break apart and form amyloid deposits.



These deposits make the heart muscle stiff, reducing its ability to relax and pump blood efficiently.



Common symptoms include:



* Shortness of breath
*  Fatigue
*  Swelling of legs
*  Irregular heartbeat
* Heart failure symptoms



Because symptoms often resemble common heart diseases, ATTR-CM can remain undiagnosed for years.







###  How Was Wainua Supposed to Work?



Wainua (eplontersen) belongs to a new generation of  **RNA-targeted medicines** called antisense oligonucleotides.



Instead of directly removing amyloid deposits, the drug works earlier in the disease pathway.



 ***Mechanism of action:***



1. Wainua binds to messenger RNA responsible for producing transthyretin.

2. It reduces production of both normal and abnormal TTR proteins in the liver.

3. Lower TTR levels may reduce the formation of new amyloid deposits.

4. Over time, this could potentially slow heart damage.



This approach represented a major advancement because it targeted the root cause of amyloid formation rather than only managing symptoms.





### What Happened in the Phase 3 Trial?



The  CARDIO-TTRansform Phase 3 trial evaluated Wainua in patients with ATTR-CM.



The study compared patients receiving eplontersen with those receiving placebo while receiving modern standard medical care.



The main goal was a composite measure:



* Cardiovascular-related death
* Recurrent cardiovascular events



After approximately 140 weeks of follow-up, the trial did  **not meet its primary endpoint.** Researchers found that adding Wainua to standard treatment did not provide a statistically significant improvement compared with placebo.







###  Why Did the Drug Fail?



The failure does not necessarily mean the drug was ineffective. Several scientific factors may explain the unexpected result.



 1. Modern background treatments may have reduced the detectable benefit



Many participants were already receiving existing ATTR therapies, including TTR stabilisers.



When patients are already benefiting from effective treatments, proving that an additional drug provides extra improvement becomes much more difficult.



The trial investigators noted that many patients were receiving stabiliser therapy, which may have influenced the ability to detect additional benefit from Wainua.





###  2. Disease biology may be more complex than expected



Reducing TTR production is scientifically logical, but ATTR-CM progression depends on multiple factors:



*  Existing amyloid deposits
*  Duration of disease
*  Heart damage before treatment
*  Patient genetics
*  Age-related changes



A drug can successfully reduce a disease-causing protein but still fail to produce measurable improvements in survival or major cardiovascular outcomes within a clinical trial period.







###  3. The trial endpoint was extremely challenging



Cardiovascular mortality is one of the hardest endpoints to improve in clinical research.



A treatment may show biological activity — such as reducing TTR levels — but demonstrating fewer deaths requires:



* Large patient populations
* Long follow-up periods
*  Strong treatment effects



Many promising cardiovascular drugs fail because the clinical benefit is smaller than expected.







 Did Wainua Show Any Positive Signals?



Although the overall trial failed, researchers observed a potential benefit in a pre-specified subgroup of patients receiving Wainua alone compared with placebo.



This finding was described as ***nominally significant*** , but further analysis is needed before drawing conclusions.



The companies plan additional evaluation of the complete dataset.







###  Impact on AstraZeneca and the Pharmaceutical Industry



The failure affected investor confidence because Wainua was expected to become an important part of AstraZeneca’s cardiovascular and metabolic disease pipeline.



Following the announcement, AstraZeneca and Ionis shares dropped significantly as markets reacted to the trial setback.



However, clinical failures are a normal part of drug development. Even large pharmaceutical companies experience setbacks because only a fraction of experimental medicines successfully reach patients.







###  What Does This Mean for ATTR-CM Patients?



The failure of Wainua does not mean progress in ATTR-CM treatment has stopped.



Other therapeutic approaches continue to develop, including:



*  TTR stabilisers
*  RNA interference therapies
*  Gene-editing approaches
*  Combination treatments



The field remains one of the fastest-growing areas in cardiovascular medicine.







###  The Future of Precision Medicine in Heart Disease



Wainua’s setback highlights an important lesson in modern medicine:



Understanding the molecular cause of a disease does not always guarantee immediate clinical success.



Precision medicine requires not only targeting the correct biological pathway but also selecting the right patients, timing treatment correctly, and measuring outcomes that truly reflect patient benefit.



As researchers continue studying ATTR-CM, future therapies may combine multiple approaches to prevent protein misfolding, remove existing deposits, and protect heart function.







###  Conclusion



AstraZeneca and Ionis’ Wainua represented one of the most advanced attempts to treat ATTR-CM through RNA-targeted therapy. Although the Phase 3 CARDIO-TTRansform trial failed to achieve its main goal, the results provide valuable information for future drug development.



The setback demonstrates the complexity of treating heart diseases at the molecular level — and why every clinical trial, successful or unsuccessful, contributes to the future of medicine.

title: A pancreatic cancer pill just did something no drug has done before.
summary: A new pill nearly doubled survival for advanced pancreatic cancer patients in a landmark trial — here's what the data actually shows.
content:
Pancreatic cancer has a reputation doctors don't sugarcoat: by the time most people are diagnosed, the disease has usually spread, and treatment options are limited. A new pill just changed one of the most stubborn numbers in oncology — how long patients actually survive.
The drug, daraxonrasib, comes from Revolution Medicines and works differently from standard chemotherapy. Instead of broadly attacking fast-dividing cells, it targets RAS — a family of proteins that, when mutated, act like a stuck accelerator pedal telling cancer cells to keep growing. Most pancreatic tumors carry a RAS mutation, which is part of why the disease is so hard to treat and why a drug built specifically to block it is a meaningful departure from business as usual.

### ***What the trial actually found***

In a global Phase 3 trial of patients whose pancreatic cancer had already progressed past a first round of chemotherapy, daraxonrasib nearly doubled how long people lived. Patients taking the daily pill had a median survival of 13.2 months, compared to 6.7 months for those on standard intravenous chemotherapy — and cut the relative risk of death by 60%. 


***No pancreatic cancer drug has ever shown a survival benefit over a full year in a late-stage trial. This one just did.


Researchers involved in the trial described the results as "practice-changing" — language that doesn't get used loosely in oncology, where incremental gains of a few weeks are often what counts as progress.***

### ***Why this matters beyond the headline number***

Pancreatic cancer's five-year survival rate sits around 13%, largely because most cases are caught after the disease has already spread and options run out quickly. A treatment that meaningfully extends survival at that late stage addresses exactly the point where current medicine struggles most.
There's also a second layer here that oncologists are watching closely: daraxonrasib is being tested not just on its own, but in combination with existing chemotherapy drugs in earlier-stage patients, where early data has shown promising tumor responses. Researchers see it less as a one-off drug and more as a foundation — a RAS-targeting approach that could eventually extend to other RAS-driven cancers, which make up a significant share of cancers overall.

## ***What happens next***

Daraxonrasib isn't approved yet. Revolution Medicines is preparing to submit this data to the FDA, aided by a "Priority Voucher" program designed to speed up review for treatments addressing major health needs — but a formal approval and public availability are still ahead, not immediate.
For patients and families dealing with a pancreatic cancer diagnosis today, this isn't a treatment available yet — it's a trial result. But it's a rare kind: a result strong enough that even researchers who study this disease for a living are using words like "unprecedented."




***Sources: Revolution Medicines (press releases, April–May 2026); CNBC; Hirshberg Foundation for Pancreatic Cancer Research; New England Journal of Medicine.***

title: "Pharmacogenomics: why your DNA might decide which drug actually works for you?"
summary: The same dose of the same drug can do nothing, work perfectly, or cause a dangerous reaction — depending on genes most patients have never been tested for.
content:
A standard dose of a standard drug doesn't work the same way in every body. Two patients with the same diagnosis, the same weight, and the same prescription can have completely different outcomes — one gets relief, one gets nothing, one ends up in the ER. For decades, that variation got chalked up to "individual response." Increasingly, it has a name: pharmacogenomics, the study of how genetic variation changes the way people process drugs. The mechanism usually comes down to enzymes, especially a family called cytochrome P450, that break drugs down in the liver. Small genetic differences change how fast those enzymes work. Some people metabolize a drug so quickly that a normal dose clears out before it can help. Others metabolize it so slowly that a normal dose builds up to toxic levels. Same pill, same prescription, opposite problem. ***Where this already changes prescribing?*** A handful of drug-gene pairs have moved from research finding to clinical practice. Clopidogrel, a blood thinner given after a stent, needs to be converted into its active form by a specific enzyme — patients with a common variant in that gene get little protective effect and remain at real risk of clotting. Certain chemotherapy drugs can cause severe, sometimes fatal toxicity in patients with a particular enzyme deficiency, which is why testing before treatment is now standard in many cancer centers. Several antidepressants and antipsychotics have dosing guidelines tied to metabolizer status, because "slow metabolizers" build up drug levels that cause side effects doctors might otherwise blame on the illness itself.

The same prescription can be the right call, the wrong call, or a dangerous one — and the difference is often written in a gene nobody checked.

***Why this isn't routine yet?*** Testing exists, and it's gotten cheaper, but it hasn't become a standard part of most prescriptions. Evidence is strong for a specific list of drug-gene pairs, not for drugs generally — pharmacogenomic testing tells you a lot about a handful of well-studied medications and very little about most others. Insurance coverage is inconsistent, results can take time labs don't always have before a prescription needs to go out, and most electronic health record systems still aren't built to flag a gene-drug interaction the way they flag an allergy. There's also a workflow problem: a test result sitting in a chart only helps if the prescribing doctor knows to look at it, and knows what it means for the specific drug in front of them. That's a smaller ask for oncology, where testing before chemotherapy is increasingly built into protocol, and a bigger one for primary care, where a single visit might touch a dozen possible prescriptions. ***What to ask about, practically ?*** If you've had a strong side effect or a drug that simply didn't work at a normal dose, it's a reasonable question for a doctor or pharmacist: is there a known gene-drug interaction for this medication, and is testing available? This is most worth raising for the drug classes where the evidence is established — certain blood thinners, some psychiatric medications, and specific chemotherapy agents — rather than as a blanket request to "test my DNA for every drug." Pharmacogenomics won't replace clinical judgment, and it isn't ready to guide every prescription. But for the specific pairs where the science is settled, it answers a question doctors have historically had to guess at: not just what to prescribe, but whether this particular body will actually respond to it.

title: The 15-minute test that could replace the lab
summary: CRISPR-based diagnostics are edging toward the clinic. Here's the case for cautious optimism.
content:
Standard PCR testing is accurate, but it's slow by design — samples get batched, run, and confirmed in a way that favors precision over speed. CRISPR-based diagnostic platforms are built around a different trade-off: near-PCR accuracy, delivered in minutes, on a device small enough for a clinic countertop rather than a reference lab. The core idea uses a CRISPR enzyme's ability to recognize a specific genetic sequence and then act as a signal amplifier once it finds a match. Instead of waiting for DNA to replicate through repeated heating and cooling cycles, the test produces a detectable signal almost as soon as binding happens. ## What's actually ready now Infectious disease panels are furthest along, with several platforms cleared for specific pathogen detection where speed changes clinical decisions — distinguishing viral from bacterial illness at the point of care, for instance. Broader panels for genetic screening are still mostly in validation studies rather than routine use.

Fast and accurate isn't the same as fast, accurate, and validated across the populations who'll actually use it. That last step is where most diagnostics quietly stall for years.

## The honest timeline Expect infectious disease applications to expand first, over the next two to three years, as more platforms clear regulatory review for specific indications. Broader genomic screening use is a longer horizon — likely five or more years — because the validation bar for a test that changes a diagnosis, rather than confirms an infection, is appropriately higher. It's a genuinely promising direction. It's just not the lab-in-a-box replacement the headlines sometimes suggest — not yet, and not for everything.

title: "Skin cancer detection apps: how good are they really — and should you trust one over a dermatologist?"
summary: Should you trust a 30-second phone scan over a dermatologist? Here's what the accuracy studies actually say.
content:
A phone scan takes thirty seconds. A dermatologist appointment can take weeks to book and ten minutes once you're in the room. So it's no surprise that skin-check apps — point your camera at a mole, get an instant risk score — have become genuinely popular. Skin cancer is also the most commonly diagnosed cancer type, and melanoma specifically goes from highly treatable to life-threatening based almost entirely on how early it's caught. That combination of convenience and stakes is exactly why it's worth looking past the app store rating and into what these tools actually get right and wrong. ## How these apps actually work Most consumer apps use a neural network trained on large libraries of labeled mole and lesion photos — the algorithm learns visual patterns associated with malignancy and scores a new photo against them. That's the entire product: your phone's camera and an algorithm, nothing else. A smaller category works differently — pairing a phone with an add-on dermatoscope lens, or built as a dedicated point-of-care device used inside a clinic alongside a physician rather than at home by a patient. That distinction between "consumer selfie app" and "clinical tool used by a professional" turns out to matter enormously, and it's the one most marketing copy blurs together.
## What the accuracy numbers actually show The best-case data looks genuinely encouraging. A prospective multicenter study of a CE-marked consumer app, checked against biopsy results, found roughly 87% sensitivity and 70% specificity for detecting pre-cancerous and cancerous lesions. In plain terms: it correctly flagged about 87 out of 100 real problem spots, and correctly cleared about 70 out of 100 harmless ones. But independent, unaffiliated researchers testing the same category of apps have repeatedly found much rougher results. One prospective study comparing an app directly to dermatologists found it classified lesions as suspicious roughly 27 times more often than the dermatologists did — a false-positive rate high enough that following the app's advice would have led to a meaningful number of unnecessary biopsies. Other independent trials found the reverse problem too: apps missing 30% or more of actual melanomas, with one review citing a 41% overall miss rate for melanoma-focused apps. A separate study found that in about 45% of cases, the app couldn't even analyze the lesion photo at all.

An app that's right most of the time is still quietly building your trust on the cases it gets wrong — and in this particular disease, the case it misses is the one visit that mattered.

## The bias problem the app store listing won't mention Most of the public image libraries used to train these models — one widely used archive is estimated to be over 70% light-skin images and under 10% dark-skin images — skew heavily toward lighter skin tones. Multiple independent studies have found models trained this way perform measurably worse at identifying malignancy on darker skin. That's a serious gap, because patients with darker skin are already more likely to be diagnosed at a later, harder-to-treat stage. Newer research models are being built specifically to close this gap, but the versions currently sitting on app stores mostly predate that work. ## Where this technology genuinely earns its place The strongest results in the research aren't from home-use selfie apps at all — they're from FDA-reviewed, point-of-care devices used inside a clinic alongside a physician. One such device, evaluated in a prospective study, matched or slightly exceeded dermatologist-level sensitivity (around 95% versus roughly 90–91%) and meaningfully cut down on missed referrals in primary care settings. The pattern across essentially every study where AI clearly helped is the same: it worked best paired with a trained clinician, not standing in for one.
## So, should you trust the app or the dermatologist? Treat a consumer app, if you use one at all, as a nudge — a reason to book an appointment sooner, never a reason to skip one. Any spot that's new, changing shape or color, itching, or bleeding deserves an in-person look regardless of what a risk score says. If you have darker skin, it's worth being extra cautious about leaning on these tools given the documented bias in their training data. Interestingly, research on patient preferences already shows most people trust a dermatologist's judgment over an app's when given the direct choice — that instinct holds up well against the evidence. The clinic-based version of this technology is genuinely promising, and it's improving quickly. But "improving quickly" and "ready to replace a trained set of eyes on your skin" are two different claims, and right now the evidence only backs the first one.

title: 3D Bioprinting of Human Organs: Can We Replace Transplants?
summary: 3D bioprinting is closing in on real tissue repair — but a fully transplantable printed organ is still years away. Here's why.
content:
Introduction

![]()

Organ transplantation is one of the greatest achievements in modern medicine, saving hundreds of thousands of lives worldwide. However, the demand for donor organs continues to exceed supply. Many patients spend years waiting for a suitable donor organ, and some die before transplantation becomes possible.

Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting has emerged as one of the most promising technologies in regenerative medicine. By combining engineering, biology, and medicine, researchers aim to create living tissues and eventually fully functional human organs that could overcome the limitations of traditional organ transplantation.

The ultimate goal of 3D bioprinting is not simply to create artificial structures, but to manufacture patient-specific organs using a person’s own cells, reducing rejection risks and eliminating dependence on organ donors.

What Is 3D Bioprinting?

3D bioprinting is an advanced manufacturing technology that uses computer-controlled printers to deposit layers of biological materials, known as bioinks, to create three-dimensional living tissue structures.

Unlike conventional 3D printing, which uses materials such as plastic or metal, bioprinting uses:

Living cells

Biomaterials

Growth factors

Extracellular matrix components

The printing process is guided by digital models created from medical imaging techniques such as CT scans and MRI.

How Does 3D Bioprinting Work?

1. Obtaining Patient Cells

Scientists can collect cells from a patient and convert them into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).

These cells can develop into different specialized cells, including:

Heart cells

Liver cells

Kidney cells

Nerve cells

Using a patient’s own cells may reduce immune rejection after implantation.

2. Creating Bioink

Bioink is the material used by a bioprinter to create tissues. It contains:

Living cells

Supporting biomaterials

Nutrients required for cell survival

Common biomaterials include:

Collagen

Gelatin

Alginate

Fibrin

An ideal bioink must provide structural support while allowing cells to grow and communicate.

3. Computer-Guided Printing

A digital model of the tissue is created using medical imaging data. The printer then deposits bioink layer by layer to build the desired structure.

Major printing methods include:

Extrusion-Based Bioprinting

The most widely used method, where bioink is pushed through a nozzle.

Inkjet Bioprinting

Uses controlled droplets of bioink to create precise structures.

Laser-Assisted Bioprinting

Uses laser energy to position cells accurately.

Current Achievements in 3D Bioprinting

Although complete transplantable human organs are not yet routinely available, researchers have achieved major progress.

1. **Bioprinted Skin**

3D-printed skin models are being developed for:

Burn treatment research

Wound healing studies

Drug testing

2. Bone and Cartilage Regeneration

Scientists are developing bioprinted scaffolds that encourage natural bone and cartilage growth.

Potential applications include:

Joint repair

Facial reconstruction

Orthopedic treatments

3. Heart Tissue

Researchers have successfully created small cardiac tissues containing living heart cells.

Future applications may include repairing damaged heart muscle after heart attacks.

4. Liver Tissue

Bioprinted liver tissues are being studied for:

Drug toxicity testing

Disease modelling

Regenerative medicine

The liver is considered one of the more promising organs because of its natural regenerative ability.

Can 3D Bioprinting Replace Organ Transplants?

The answer is possibly in the future, but major challenges remain.

A fully functional artificial organ requires:

Correct anatomical structure

Multiple specialized cell types

Blood vessel networks

Nerve connections

Long-term survival after implantation

Creating a small tissue sample is much easier than producing a complex organ such as a kidney, heart, or lung.

Major Challenges

1. Vascularization

The biggest challenge is creating blood vessel networks.

Large tissues require a constant supply of oxygen and nutrients. Without blood vessels, printed organs cannot survive after implantation.

Researchers are developing artificial vascular systems, but this remains a major obstacle.

2. Organ Complexity

Human organs contain millions of cells arranged in highly organized structures.

For example, the kidney contains complex filtering units that are extremely difficult to reproduce artificially.

3. Cell Maturation

Printed cells often require time and biological signals to mature and function like natural cells.

4. Large-Scale Manufacturing

Producing a complete human organ requires:

Advanced bioprinters

Large numbers of healthy cells

Strict quality control

Reliable manufacturing methods

Future Applications

Personalized Organ Replacement

Future patients may receive organs created from their own cells, reducing:

Organ rejection

Waiting lists

Dependence on donors

Drug Development

Bioprinted human tissues could improve drug testing by providing realistic models of human organs.

This may:

Reduce animal testing

Improve safety predictions

Speed up medicine development

Disease Research

Scientists can create patient-specific disease models to study conditions and develop targeted treatments.

Future Outlook

3D bioprinting is unlikely to completely replace organ transplantation immediately. However, it may gradually transform regenerative medicine.

Early applications will likely include:

Tissue repair

Small tissue implants

Drug testing models

Partial organ replacement

Fully functional printed organs such as kidneys, hearts, and lungs remain a long-term goal, but advances in stem cell technology, artificial intelligence, and biomaterials are bringing this possibility closer.

Conclusion

3D bioprinting represents a revolutionary approach to solving the global organ shortage crisis. Although researchers have not yet achieved routine printing of complete transplantable organs, progress is accelerating rapidly.

The future may bring a time when patients receive personalized organs created from their own cells, transforming transplantation from a donor-dependent system into a technology-driven medical solution.

The question is no longer whether humans can print biological tissues — but how soon we can print fully functional organs.

References

The Lancet — Developments in transplantation and regenerative therapies

Science Translational Medicine — Tissue engineering and organ fabrication research

National Institutes of Health (NIH) — Regenerative medicine research programs

title: AI models can read X-rays fast. Should they read them alone?
summary: A look at what the accuracy numbers actually mean once you account for how radiologists work in practice.
content:
Over the past two years, a wave of imaging models has posted accuracy numbers that, on paper, match or beat average radiologist performance on specific tasks — spotting a fracture, flagging a nodule, triaging a chest film for urgency. Vendors like to lead with those numbers. What they mention less is what "accuracy" was measured against. Most benchmark studies compare a model against a single read, on a curated dataset, with a clear ground truth established after the fact. Real clinical work looks nothing like that. A radiologist reading a chest film at 2am is working from a messy history, an inconsistent machine, and a patient who doesn't fit the training distribution. ## Where the models genuinely help The strongest evidence isn't for replacement — it's for triage and second opinion. Models that flag likely-urgent studies for earlier review have shown real reductions in time-to-diagnosis for conditions like pneumothorax and intracranial hemorrhage. That's a workflow improvement, not a diagnostic one, and it's still valuable.

The question was never "can a model read a film." It's whether a model plus a clinician beats a clinician alone — and on that, the evidence is much thinner than the headlines suggest.

## What to watch for If you're evaluating a tool for your own practice, ask for performance data broken out by the equipment and population you'll actually be using it on — not just its overall benchmark score. A model tuned on one manufacturer's scanner can behave differently on another. That detail rarely makes it into a sales deck, but it's the one that determines whether the tool holds up in your hands. None of this is an argument against the technology. It's an argument for reading past the top-line number before it changes how you practice.

title: Continuous glucose monitors are coming for people without diabetes
summary: Why metabolic wearables are moving into general wellness — and what the evidence does and doesn't support.
content:
Continuous glucose monitors were built for one job: helping people with diabetes manage insulin dosing without finger sticks. That's still their best-supported use. But over the last few years, a second market has grown up around them — healthy adults wearing a CGM to "optimize" energy, sleep, or weight, with no diabetes diagnosis at all. The appeal is obvious. A glucose curve is a number you can watch move in real time, and that feedback loop is satisfying in a way that annual bloodwork isn't. Whether it's clinically useful for someone with normal glucose regulation is a separate question. ## What the data actually shows Glucose variability in people without diabetes is wide and mostly unremarkable — spikes after refined carbs are normal physiology, not evidence of dysfunction. Most consumer CGM apps have no way to distinguish a meaningful pattern from ordinary variation, so they tend to flag both.

A device can be genuinely useful for one population and mostly noise for another. The hardware doesn't change — the interpretation does.

## Where it's reasonable to consider one For people with prediabetes, strong family history, or specific metabolic concerns their physician is already tracking, a short monitoring period can add real information a single fasting glucose test misses. Used that way — as a defined-duration diagnostic tool rather than a permanent accessory — a CGM earns its place. The technology isn't the problem. Treating a continuous data stream as inherently more meaningful than a single good test, without asking what question it's actually answering, is.
